Exercise 1: Deduce Quarto features
Check out the appearance and contents of this document. Thoughts?
It looks like a normal webpage. Some words are bolded and are made to stand out. There are different text sizes too for emphasis.
In the toolbar at the top of this document, Render the .qmd file into a .html file. Where is this file stored? Thoughts about its appearance / contents? Can you edit it?
This file is stored in my ica folder (which is then in my portfolio). The appearance is plain and it’s contents are informational. I can edit it here. To see my changes, I render it again.
Toggling between the .qmd and .html files, explain the purpose of the following features in the .qmd file:
* test This one italics the word between.
** test This one bolds the word between.
# #test This one doesn’t change the word’s appearance. The # symbol just shows up where I typed it.
- -test- -test This one doesn’t change the appearance of the word, The dashes show up where I typed them.
\  \test\ Only the first test showed up. The others disappeared. The backward slashes don’t change the appearance of the word.
![](url)  This one put the word in the brackets into a box. It might work as a link? Maybe I didn’t do it right…

title: My first Quarto document
text:
Exercise 3: Chunks
Quarto isn’t a mind reader – we must distinguish R code from text. We do so by putting code inside an R chunk:

Codeseq(from = 100, to = 1000, by = 50)

 [1]  100  150  200  250  300  350  400  450  500  550  600  650  700  750  800
[16]  850  900  950 1000



Put the seq() code in the chunk.
Press the green arrow in the top right of the chunk. What happens in the qmd? In the qmd, the code works! It’s doing what it’s suppposed to do.
Render. What appears in the html: R code, output, or both? Both! I see the R code and the outputs.

title: My first Quarto document

Exercise 4: Practice

Use R code to create the following sequence: 10 10 10 10
Store the sequence as four_tens.
Use an R function (which we haven’t learned!) to add up the numbers in four_tens.


Coderep(t=4, x=10)

[1] 10 10 10 10



Codefour_tens<-rep(t=4, x=10)



Codefour_tens

[1] 10 10 10 10



Code10+10+10+10

[1] 40



Codesum(rep(t=4,x=10))

[1] 40

title: My first Quarto document
text:
Exercise 6: Comments
Run the chunk below. Notice that R ignores anything in a line starting with a pound sign (#). If we took the # away we’d get an error!

Code# This is a comment
4 + 5

[1] 9


We’ll utilize this feature to comment our code, i.e. leave short notes about what our code is doing. Below, replace the ??? with an appropriate comment.

Code# Storing the temps
temperature_c <- 10
temperature_f <- temperature_c * 9/5 + 32
temperature_f

[1] 50
